title: Prosecco and Asti
subtitle: Italy's lighter bubbles
objectives: Explain how Asti keeps its sweetness

steps.title: Prosecco
steps.body: Prosecco comes from north-east Italy, in the Veneto and Friuli. It must be at least 85% Glera. Most is made by the tank method, giving pear, apple and white flower aromas, light body and fresh acidity. The top area is Conegliano Valdobbiadene, a DOCG of steep hills, with the single slope of Cartizze at its peak.
steps.highlight: Glera, tank method, pear and flowers

steps.title: Asti
steps.body: Asti and Moscato d'Asti come from Piedmont and are made from Moscato Bianco. Instead of a second fermentation, the juice is chilled and stored, then fermented once in a sealed tank. Fermentation is stopped by cooling and filtering, leaving sugar and only 5 to 7% alcohol. Asti is fully sparkling; Moscato d'Asti is gently fizzy, frizzante.

steps.prompt: Asti is made with a second fermentation, like Prosecco.
steps.explanation: Not true. Asti uses a single fermentation in a sealed tank, stopped early to keep sugar and low alcohol.

steps.title: Serving them
steps.body: Both are made to drink young and well chilled. Prosecco suits aperitifs and light dishes; Extra Dry is the most common style, slightly sweeter than Brut. Moscato d'Asti, sweet and low in alcohol, suits fruit desserts and, in Piedmont, sometimes breakfast pastries.

steps.prompt: Which grape is the main grape of Prosecco?
steps.explanation: Prosecco must be at least 85% Glera. Moscato Bianco is the grape of Asti.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Prosecco is mostly Glera, made by the tank method
Asti and Moscato d'Asti come from one fermentation, stopped early
Both are best young and chilled
